description: Soft sourdough sandwich bread at 65% hydration, with milk, butter, and honey. Work out the amounts for any flour weight, with the table and pan notes.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 275 g milk, 100 g starter, 10 g salt, 40 g butter, and 25 g honey. Total dough 900 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of liquid.
Total liquid is 65% of the flour: 500 × 0.65 = 325 g. Milk to add is 325 - 50 = 275 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.
examples.title: 500 g flour sandwich loaf

examples.result: Add 540 g flour, 330 g milk, 120 g starter, 12 g salt, 48 g butter, and 30 g honey. Total dough 1080 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 600 × 0.20 = 120 g.
The starter brings 60 g of flour and 60 g of liquid.
Total liquid is 65% of the flour: 600 × 0.65 = 390 g. Milk to add is 390 - 60 = 330 g.
Flour to add is 600 - 60 = 540 g. Salt is 2%: 600 × 0.02 = 12 g.
examples.title: 600 g flour sandwich loaf, large pan

faqs.answer: Milk counts as liquid, so it replaces the water in the hydration maths. Whole milk is about 87% water, and for a sandwich loaf the difference is small enough to ignore: weigh the milk where the calculator says water. The milk fat and sugars are what make the crumb soft and the crust tender.
faqs.question: Does milk count as water in the hydration?

faqs.answer: Yes, if you want a softer crumb. Published sandwich recipes run from about 60% to 70% liquid, with 5 to 12% butter and 3 to 9% sugar or honey. This calculator uses 65% liquid, 8% butter, and 5% honey, which sits in the middle of that range. More butter makes a richer loaf; less makes a chewier one.
faqs.question: Can I change the butter and honey amounts?

faqs.answer: A 500 g flour loaf makes about 900 g of dough, which fits a standard 9 by 5 inch pan. A 600 g flour loaf makes about 1080 g of dough, which fits a 10 by 5 inch pan. If the dough fills more than two thirds of the pan before rising, it will overflow: use a bigger pan or scale down.
faqs.question: What size pan fits this loaf?

faqs.answer: Bake at 375°F for 40 to 45 minutes, until the top is golden and the inside reads 190°F on a thermometer. Enriched loaves are done at a lower temperature than lean loaves, which need 200 to 210°F, because the milk and butter keep the crumb moist.
faqs.question: How long do I bake a sourdough sandwich loaf?

faqs.answer: Yes. Replace the milk with the same weight of oat milk and the butter with the same weight of softened coconut oil or a vegan block. The crumb stays tender because the fat percentage is unchanged. Honey can swap for the same weight of sugar or maple syrup.
faqs.question: Can I make this dairy free?

felicityNote: This is the loaf my kids actually eat. The crust is soft enough for small teeth, the slices are square, and it makes a sandwich that does not fall apart in a lunchbox.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total liquid as a share of total flour. At 65%, every 100 g of flour holds 65 g of liquid, and here the liquid is milk.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.
Softened butter, 8% of the flour. It coats the gluten and makes the crumb tender. The table lists it for each flour weight.
Honey, 5% of the flour. It feeds the fermentation, browns the crust, and holds moisture. The table lists it for each flour weight.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Milk to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %. Butter = flour × 8%. Honey = flour × 5%.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and milk
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the milk to add. Warm the milk to about 80°F first. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter, honey, and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, the honey, and the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left, then rest for 20 minutes so the flour hydrates.

howToSteps.name: Work in the butter
howToSteps.text: Add the softened butter a little at a time and mix or knead until it is fully worked in and the dough is smooth and supple. An enriched dough is easier in a mixer, but it can be done by hand.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, then shape it into a log and place it seam side down in a greased 9 by 5 inch pan. Let it rise again until it crowns just above the rim.

howToSteps.name: Bake at 375°F
howToSteps.text: Bake for 40 to 45 minutes, until the top is golden and the inside reads 190°F. Cool in the pan for 10 minutes, then turn out and cool fully before slicing.

lede: A sourdough sandwich loaf is an enriched dough: milk instead of water, butter and honey for a soft crumb, and a lower hydration that shapes easily into a pan. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter.

title: Sourdough Sandwich Loaf Calculator
tutorial: A sandwich loaf is a different kind of sourdough. A lean boule is flour, water, starter, and salt, and it eats chewy with a crackling crust. A sandwich loaf adds milk, butter, and honey, and it eats soft: a tender crumb, a thin crust, and slices that hold a filling without tearing. The enrichment is the whole point, and it is what makes this loaf disappear from a lunchbox.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 500 g of total flour at 65% hydration, the dough holds 325 g of liquid in total, and here the liquid is milk. Your starter brings 50 g of that liquid, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 275 g of milk to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g, butter is 8%, which is 40 g, and honey is 5%, which is 25 g.

Milk counts as liquid in the hydration maths. Whole milk is about 87% water, and for a sandwich loaf the difference is small enough to ignore: weigh the milk where the calculator says water. The milk fat and sugars are what make the crumb fine and pale and the crust soft and golden. If you want a dairy-free loaf, swap the milk for the same weight of oat milk and the butter for the same weight of softened coconut oil. The crumb stays tender because the fat percentage is unchanged.

The numbers here sit in the middle of the published range. Across the sandwich recipes I checked, liquid runs from about 60% to 70% of the flour, butter from 5% to 12%, and sugar or honey from 3% to 9%. This calculator uses 65% liquid, 8% butter, and 5% honey. More butter makes a richer loaf, closer to a pain de mie. Less butter makes a chewier loaf, closer to a lean pan bread. The table lists the butter and honey for each flour weight, so scaling is just reading a row.

Bake it cooler and shorter than a boule: 375°F for 40 to 45 minutes, until the top is golden and the inside reads 190°F on a thermometer. Enriched loaves are done at a lower temperature than lean loaves, which need 200 to 210°F, because the milk and butter keep the crumb moist. Cool the loaf fully before slicing, or the crumb will compress under the knife. A 500 g flour loaf makes about 900 g of dough, which fits a standard 9 by 5 inch pan.
